summary: DeepRepoQA answers developer questions about a repository with a four-role LLM loop (perception, planning, execution, evaluation) driven by Monte-Carlo Tree Search over six actions: AST name lookups (FindClass/FindFunction/FindCodeSnippet), voyage-code-3 SemanticSearch, ViewCode and Finish. Answers must cite file and line spans. On SWE-QA (720 questions, 15 Python repos), scored by a three-LLM judge panel, it beats embedding-RAG baselines by 4 to 12 points out of 100 and the best ReAct agent baseline by 0.9 to 4.7 points across four backbones. A commercial agent (Cursor auto mode) still scores highest.

claims.claim: DeepRepoQA outperforms state-of-the-art ReAct-style agents on all backbones (largest gain 7.08 over SWE-agent on Qwen3-Coder)
claims.evidence: Table 2: 65.90 vs 65.02 OpenHands (GLM-4.6, +0.88), 68.71 vs 65.30 (Kimi K2, +3.41), 64.43 vs 62.33 (Qwen3-Coder, +2.10), 70.06 vs 65.39 SWE-agent (GPT-5.1, +4.67). The 7.08 figure is vs SWE-agent, which on Qwen3-Coder is beaten even by Function-Chunking RAG (57.35 vs 61.13). Single run per cell, no CIs; the judge-vs-human MAE (5.22 points, App. C.3) is larger than three of the four margins over the best agent.

claims.claim: Surpasses or matches leading commercial tools (Cursor, Tongyi Lingma) when using GPT-5.1 and Kimi K2
claims.evidence: Table 2: GPT-5.1 70.06 vs Cursor 70.71 and Tongyi 69.12. Kimi K2 68.71 is below both commercial tools, so the Kimi half of the claim is not supported. Commercial tools ran without iteration or cost limits. The Java subset (App. D) also has Cursor on top (65.10 vs 63.29).

claims.claim: Consistent 4-7% improvements over SOTA agent baselines across multiple LLMs (Conclusion)
claims.evidence: Holds only against SWE-agent (+4.84, +6.35, +7.08, +4.67). Against OpenHands the gains are +0.88, +3.41, +2.10, +5.84. Against the best agent per backbone they are 0.9 to 4.7 points.

claims.claim: MCTS is the primary driver and every component is essential
claims.evidence: Table 3 uses one backbone (Qwen3-Coder) and one run: w/o MCTS -2.27 (62.16, about OpenHands level), w/o Evaluation Agent -3.50 (the largest drop, so the value-estimating LLM call matters more than MCTS itself), w/o Perception -1.73, w/o SemanticSearch -1.07. All deltas are smaller than judge MAE. Removing MCTS raises Relevance and Clarity. The text also misreports a Reasoning delta ('+0.07' should be +4.07).

claims.claim: Computational efficiency comparable to state-of-the-art agents and commercial tools
claims.evidence: Table B1 average input/output tokens: DeepRepoQA 78.7K/6.2K, OpenHands 87.0K/1.9K, SWE-agent 126K/4.6K, Cursor 129K/1.6K. RAG baselines use about 5-6K tokens (roughly 13x fewer) and reach 56-63 points. No latency or dollar cost reported; App. E.7 mentions a single 332 s run that hit the node cap.

claims.claim: The LLM judge panel is reliable
claims.evidence: App. C: 60 questions x 6 systems, GPT-5.1 answers only, 3 human experts. Consensus Pearson r = 0.972, pairwise preference agreement 88.2% (kappa 0.725), Clarity alpha only 0.32-0.41. The 'inter-method gap ~25 pts' used to justify MAE 5.22 does not match the actual 1-5 point gaps between the top systems. Judges also penalise valid alternative designs (F4).

patterns.note: Comparison is reasonable: the same four backbones run with two embedding-RAG pipelines (voyage-code-3, top-10, function or sliding-window chunks) versus exploration agents. Exploration agents win on all four backbones (DeepRepoQA +4.0 to +11.9 over the best RAG; the one exception is SWE-agent on Qwen3-Coder, which loses to RAG). The cost is about 13x more tokens. Python OSS, LLM-judged, single run. The MCTS-specific margin over a plain ReAct agent is small (0.9-4.7) and the commercial Cursor agent is still best.

Removing SemanticSearch costs only 1.07 points (Table 3, one backbone, no variance). Failure modes F1/F2 (App. E) come from embeddings returning semantically similar but literally wrong code, and on ambiguous wording every MCTS branch inherits the same wrong first hit. Standalone embedding RAG trails agentic exploration by 4-12 points.

AST name lookups (FindClass/FindFunction with file_pattern) are the precision tools. In a post-hoc look at the error analysis, 80% of top-scoring answers used symbol anchoring and all reached the right file within two hops (App. E.3). A lexical-only arm (w/o SemanticSearch) loses only 1.07, but no semantic-only arm exists, so lexical retrieval is not isolated.

Perception, Planning, Execution and Evaluation role prompts. Ablations remove the Perception (-1.73) and Evaluation (-3.50) roles on a single backbone with no variance. Each node costs four LLM calls, which shows up as 3x the output tokens of OpenHands.

Two uses. (1) An LLM evaluation agent acts as the MCTS value function; removing it is the largest ablation drop. (2) A three-LLM judge panel is validated against three humans: high consensus correlation, but MAE 5.22 is coarser than most headline margins, Clarity is unreliable, and a single reference answer penalises valid alternative designs.

Question types include architecture exploration, design rationale, dependency tracing and feature location (Table 5), which is the code side of pre-spec discovery. Docs, tickets and people are not used, and nothing feeds a spec.

The planning prompt says 'you cannot communicate with the user'. Failure mode F2 (an ambiguous phrase like 'structured container' leading all 17 nodes to the wrong class) is exactly where a clarifying question would help, but this is not tested.
Motivated by developers needing to understand codebases, but no developer study. Answers carry file:line citations, which helps human verification, but comprehension is not measured.
SWE-QA comes from the same first author (Peng et al. 2026); the authors added three SWE-Bench-Live repos.

methodology.sample: SWE-QA: 720 QA pairs over 15 Python repos (576 original + 3 repos added by the authors from SWE-Bench-Live). Java subset: 30 QA pairs over 3 repos. Human validation: 60 questions x 6 systems.
methodology.baselines: Direct prompting; Function-Chunking and Sliding-Window RAG (voyage-code-3, top-10); SWE-agent v1.0 and OpenHands 1.1.0 adapted to QA with a 15-iteration cap; Tongyi Lingma and Cursor-agent auto mode with no limits
methodology.models: GLM-4.6, Kimi K2, Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B, GPT-5.1. Judges: GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro.
methodology.variance: Single run per configuration (exploration temperature 0.7); no CIs or significance tests on system scores; bootstrap CI only for judge-human correlation
methodology.ablations: Four component removals and a 5-30 node budget sweep, all on Qwen3-Coder only
methodology.contamination_controls: Retrieval-free baseline; three newer SWE-Bench-Live repos. Claims of 'less popular repositories' sit awkwardly with scikit-learn and Sphinx in the set.
methodology.languages: Python (main); Java (30 questions, backbone not stated)

standards.artifacts: Code and data on GitHub and Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21063159); all prompts in App. F

biases.detail: The benchmark (SWE-QA) is the first author's own, extended by the authors, and scored with the authors' rubric and judge panel.
One run per cell despite temperature 0.7 exploration. Margins of 0.9-4.7 points over the best agent have no uncertainty estimate.
Judge-human MAE (5.22) exceeds most headline differences. App. C.3 justifies it with a ~25 point inter-method gap that does not exist among the top systems.
'Consistent 4-7% improvements over SOTA agent baselines' and 'all components essential with no redundancy' overstate Table 2 and Table 3.
Main results are Python only. The Java check is 30 questions with an unspecified backbone.
Popular repos (scikit-learn, Sphinx) are likely in pretraining. The direct-prompting baseline helps but does not remove the risk that agents verify memorised answers faster.
Tokens are reported, but no latency or dollar cost, although MCTS needs four LLM calls per node.

coi.affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, HKUST, UC San Diego
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Cursor and Tongyi Lingma as baselines (no author affiliation)
coi.detail: Academic authors, but they also own the benchmark the system is ranked on. No vendor product promoted.

verdict_reason: Four backbones, reasonable RAG and agent baselines, human-validated judges, released code and prompts, and an honest error analysis. But it is single-run, on a self-built Python benchmark, the MCTS margin over a plain agent is within judge error, and the conclusion and intro overstate gains over the best agent and parity with commercial tools. What survives is that agentic exploration beats embedding RAG for repo QA, plus the qualitative success and failure patterns.
applicability: For an onboarding or discovery assistant over the team's Java ingestion repos, this supports giving developers an exploring agent rather than a chat-over-embeddings index. It does not justify building MCTS: the host agents the team already runs (Cursor auto, and by extension Claude Code or Codex) match or beat it. The portable findings are harness rules for the host agent: (1) anchor on symbol lookups (LSP/AST/Gortex) with a path filter before semantic search; (2) re-read the cited source right before answering; (3) require file:line citations; (4) for 'where is X' questions, check that the literal identifier appears in the cited span; (5) when a domain term is ambiguous, look it up in a glossary or ask, because all search branches inherit a wrong first interpretation. Nothing here tests cross-repo questions (ingestion to delivery contracts), Spring wiring or configuration-driven behaviour, all central for the team. The team would need its own small human-labelled question set, since LLM-judge resolution is about 5 points.

conflicts_with.detail: CodeNib finds dense retrieval beats BM25 by about 17 points file Recall@10 and on repair. Here removing SemanticSearch from an agent with AST name lookups costs only 1.07 points on QA. The two may reconcile because the lexical arm here is symbol lookup, not BM25, and the task is QA, not localisation.
